session_meta.research_objective:
Focus group guide exploring how men in the UK make everyday food
choices, how social context, work, hobbies, health, taste and other
people shape what they eat, how gender and masculinity may influence
food choices, and what would need to change for plant-based foods to
become more acceptable or appealing.
session_meta.topic_domain: Masculinity, food choice, animal product consumption, and plant-based eating
session_meta.participant_collective_identity: Men in the UK reflecting on food choices, male friendship, gender norms, and plant-based eating
session_meta.moderator_knowledge_brief:
Explore (1) everyday food decision-making, (2) the social contexts in
which men spend time with male friends, (3) the influence of other
people, work, hobbies, health, nutrition and taste on food choices,
(4) whether participants perceive gender as shaping what they eat,
(5) social acceptability and gendered meanings attached to vegetarian,
vegan, plant-based, feminine or masculine foods, and (6) what personal,
social and practical changes would make plant-based eating more viable
or appealing. The discussion should remain exploratory, non-judgmental,
and non-leading.

initial_session_plan.thematisation_approach: I will frame participants as men reflecting on their own everyday lives — the places they go, the food they eat, the company they keep — without priming any gender or food-ideology framing up front. The opening sections will let them speak as individuals with concrete routines before any more charged questions arise. I will avoid any collective identity label that could prime defensiveness or social desirability.
priority_research_areas: Gender and food choice (Section 3): This is the section most likely to produce socially performative or abstractly reasoned answers. Participants may deny gender influence in principle while describing clearly gendered behaviour in practice. Behavioural grounding and contradiction-surfacing will be the key tools here.

Plant-based shift and barriers (Section 4): The hypothetical framing ('imagine you decided...') risks producing fantasy-mode answers rather than grounded ones. I will need to anchor responses to specific real moments — meals, contexts, social situations — rather than abstract conditions for change.

Social acceptability and gendered food meanings (threading across Sections 3–5): Participants may self-censor on this topic in a group setting, particularly if they sense peer judgment. Consensus risk will be elevated; I will need to watch for social convergence and use invite_dissent carefully.

What would make plant-based more appealing (Section 5): This section can drift into generic market-research territory. I will push for personal, specific, socially contextualised answers rather than product-feature lists.

known_risk_conditions: Social desirability bias is high throughout: Men in a group setting may understate the role of gender in their choices and may perform pragmatic indifference to both meat and plant-based foods rather than reveal genuine attitudes. Use behavioural grounding early and often.

Consensus risk is structural: This is a five-man group discussing a topic where strong peer norms exist. Participants may converge quickly, especially on plant-based scepticism or on denying gender effects. Plan invite_dissent for Sections 3–5.

Hypothetical drift in Section 4: The 'imagine you decided' framing risks producing wishful or policy-mode answers. Ground with: 'Think about a specific meal or situation — what would have had to be different?'
Tangent risk in Section 1: Male friendship and place is a warm opener but could generate long social storytelling that eats into the time budget. Keep it light and move on.

Time pressure: 45 minutes for 6 substantive sections is tight. Sections 1 and 2 are scene-setters, not research targets. I must resist over-probing in context sections and prioritise depth in Sections 3–5.
initial_session_plan.directivity_plan: Sections 0–2 (intro and context): Light touch. Allow natural self-introduction and storytelling. Probe only if something genuinely rich surfaces; do not over-excavate these sections. Section 3 (gender and food): Increase directivity. Push hard for behavioural specificity. Surface contradictions. Use reflect_contradiction and invite_dissent when warranted. Section 4 (plant-based shift): Moderate-high directivity. Anchor hypotheticals in real moments. Push past first-level answers about cost or taste. Section 5 (making plant-based appealing): Moderate directivity. Allow some generative breadth but steer away from generic marketing answers. Section 6 (closing): Light touch. Space for anything overlooked. Do not reopen closed threads.

time_budget.budget_rationale: Sections 3, 4, and 5 are the main research-bearing sections and together receive roughly 65% of the word budget. Sections 1 and 2 are context-builders and receive a moderate share. Section 0 (intro) and Section 6 (closing) are lightest. Per-section turn budgets are estimates based on five participants; actual moderator turns will be a minority of these.

section_summaries.section_label: Opening discussion: male friendship and place
section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section centered on the psychology of place loyalty — why familiar venues persist despite abundant alternatives. A key distinction emerged organically: belonging-through-recognition (the social glue of shared regulars and staff familiarity) versus belonging-through-invisibility (the relief of existing without performing or explaining oneself). The first framing dominated the Henry-Connor exchange; Bilal's contribution usefully complicated it, introducing a more solitary, low-stakes version of attachment that Connor then acknowledged as genuinely distinct.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The moderator largely stood back during the Henry-Connor exchange, correctly allowing a productive theme to develop before intervening to widen participation. The redirect to Sam, Noah, and Bilal by name was well-timed and surfaced Bilal's contrasting perspective, which enriched the section considerably. Sam and Noah remained unheard, which is a gap. The transition to everyday food decision-making was clean but slightly abrupt — the belonging-versus-invisibility distinction had more potential that was left unexplored.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section introduced a structural distinction that cut across the earlier belonging/invisibility framing: constrained choice versus habitual default. Noah's pushback on Sam's 'default mechanism' argument sharpened a genuinely useful typology — Connor chooses familiarity despite options; Noah has no options to choose between. The section resolved this tension productively through peer dialogue rather than moderator intervention, landing on geography and availability as a variable that complicates any unified account of food habit.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The moderator stayed almost entirely absent while Noah and Sam worked through a real disagreement — correctly so, since the exchange was substantive and self-correcting. The transition out was clean and timely, acknowledging the distinction Noah surfaced without over-elaborating it. The risk is that Henry, Connor, and Bilal were silent throughout; the section was effectively a two-person exchange. The pivot to gender was appropriate but slightly abrupt given the momentum still present.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section centered on the social regulation of food choice among men — specifically, the unspoken norms governing what feels safe to order in male company. A productive tension emerged between Bilal's agentic framing (awareness enables choice) and Sam's structural pushback (knowing it doesn't matter doesn't dissolve the feeling). The section converged on context-dependence over age or individual will, with geography, familiarity, and anonymity all modulating how strongly masculine food-coding operates.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The moderator largely held back while Bilal and Henry developed an age-versus-context distinction, intervening twice — first to widen to the quieter three, which successfully drew in Sam, Connor, and Noah; second to pivot toward explicit gendered food categories, which produced useful but somewhat predictable responses. Connor and Noah's entries felt slightly thin. The transition to the plant-based hypothetical was clean and well-timed, capitalising on the section's implicit question: if the awareness is structural, what would it actually take to override it?

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section tested the earlier belonging/constraint framing against a concrete hypothetical — going plant-based — and produced a consistent finding: the barrier is social visibility, not practical feasibility. A useful distinction crystallised between momentary deviation (ordering a salad once) and ongoing identity-marking (being the plant-based guy), with participants converging on motivation threshold as the real variable: constraints only function as constraints when there is something you actually want.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The moderator largely let the Noah-Connor exchange develop without interference, correctly — it was substantive and self-correcting. The follow-up challenge to Henry's apparent contradiction was well-placed and produced a genuinely clarifying response. Widening to Sam and Bilal by name was necessary but yielded thinner, convergent contributions rather than new perspectives. The section risk is that five participants landed on broadly similar positions; the transition question about appeal rather than barriers was a sound attempt to reopen the space.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section produced a rare convergence: all five participants independently caught themselves rationalising avoidance — attributing discomfort to practical constraints, geography, or indifference when the underlying mechanism was unwillingness to sustain visible difference. The section sharpened a distinction already implicit in earlier sections: single deviation is manageable; ongoing pattern-marking is not. Constant, unavoidable public visibility of food choice emerged as the specific feature that makes plant-based eating categorically harder than other lifestyle divergences.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The moderator's key intervention — pressing Henry on the contradiction between claiming not to care and articulating in detail why visibility would matter — triggered a productive cascade of self-correction that spread voluntarily to Sam, Noah, and Bilal without further prompting. Staying out of the Henry-Sam exchange was correct. The one structural risk is that Connor, whose framing opened the section, was not revisited after Henry's rebuttal — his perspective on whether the self-correction landed for him went uncaptured.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section served as a brief but significant coda: Connor voluntarily collapsed the geographic exceptionalism he had maintained throughout the session, recognising it as a variant of the same rationalisation pattern others had named. The section produced no new themes but completed a symmetry — every participant had now publicly acknowledged the same underlying mechanism, with Connor's self-correction landing as confirmation that the visibility-as-barrier finding held across different contexts, not just constrained ones.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The moderator correctly recognised that Connor's self-correction was a natural closing beat and used it as one, offering a brief synthesis before opening the floor for anything unsaid. The risk is that the close came quickly after a single turn — Sam, Noah, Henry, and Bilal were not invited to respond to Connor's reframe, which might have added texture. But given time constraints and the convergent state of the group, ending on that note rather than reopening was a reasonable call.
